articles.content_orig:
Five men arrested on suspicion of terror offences near RAF Fairford on Sunday morning are UK nationals in their 20s who live in London , police say
They were arrested under the Explosives Act and on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act - BBC Verify has looked at the "company" vans seen nearby
Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator Vicki Evans says she is "very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised"
Earlier, a farmer who called 999 when she saw "a large group of hooded and masked men" said she "foiled" their plans - here's the WhatsApp she sent her neighbours at 01:49 on Sunday
But Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the farmer only had a "partial picture" , while declining to speculate on possible Iranian links
The RAF base is used by the US military. President Trump said the US had the five men "under view for a long time, and we got them"
One person who lives near the base tells us that local people were sent home by armed police just hours before the suspects were arrested - others say security had ramped up days before
Edited by Steve Mellen, Katie Jaffar and Owen Amos with Nick Johnson and Edward Rowe reporting from RAF Fairford
Villagers have been speaking to the BBC about what was happening around RAF Fairford in the days leading up to the arrests on Sunday.
Here's a reminder of what they said:
Although Whitehall sources have told the BBC the operation at RAF Fairford was not "intelligence-led", these accounts from local residents suggest that authorities might have been anticipating something happening at the base before Sunday's arrests.
By Benedict Garman and Charlotte Green
After a major incident near RAF Fairford was declared by police on Sunday, BBC Verify began geolocating images and videos from the scene, mapping key locations to help understand what was happening and where.
We first plotted where police had put roadblocks in place on three routes leading into the village of Whelford. This helped us narrow down where the main areas of police activity were focused.
The police said a 400m cordon had been put in place around three suspicious vehicles - which matched the position of the roadblocks.
We also verified a photo showing five men sitting in the road who had apparently been detained by police.
A hedge, signpost and telephone box cross-referenced against Google Street View placed them in a road about 350m from one of the runway access gates at RAF Fairford.
Another image showed two bomb disposal lorries which we matched to a spot roughly 300m away from the runway gate. Street View also helped place the location of a security camera image showing the three white vans.
Later, live helicopter video from the scene revealed where the bomb disposal teams were operating.
The location of this photograph of arrested men has been verified by the BBC
Emma Hallett Reporting from the scene
The farmer who has been speaking to the media about what unfolded in the early hours of Sunday says she had been out at a party âmuch laterâ than she would usually be out.
She says she noticed three vans were parked in a âweird formationâ in a âloopâ in the village of Whelford.
âWhen you live in Whelford, you notice everything,â she says, adding that all the villagers know each other, including what cars they drive.
She describes the vans as having âstrange signageâ on them.
âI looked at it and thought âthat is not realâ,â she says.
She stopped and looked at the vans as well as trying to call the phone number of the side of the van â which did not work.
The farmer raised the alarm in a neighbours' group Whatsapp
As she turned around she says she saw a âlarge groupâ of men who then started to âpanicâ.
She says she thought she had âdazzled themâ.
The woman says the men were all wearing similar clothing and they had their faces covered.
She then called the MoD Police and base liaison number.
âThe phone rang and rang and rang,â she says, so she phoned 999 and let people in the village know what was happening.
âLiterally within five minutes it all kicked off," she adds. "There were armed police, a helicopter.â
Emma Hallett Reporting from the scene
A huge police operation was launched after the farmer's 999 call in the early hours of Sunday morning
A farmer who says she called 999 sparking the police response to the incident at RAF Fairford says she is â100% certainâ she saw between eight and 10 people who fled into trees when they spotted her.
The local resident told the BBC earlier she had seen three white vans blocking a road and "a large group of hooded and masked men".
The woman adds she could tell they âweren't localsâ, but that was because of their behaviour âmore than how they lookedâ, saying they had their faces covered.
Reflecting on the fact that five people have been arrested, she says this is something that continues to concern her.
The woman also says she is surprised she has not yet been contacted by anyone in an official capacity about what she saw.
CTP Senior National Coordinator, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans also addresses possible motives behind yesterday's incident, saying that officers investigating it should be given the space to "work carefully and clearly".
"I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised," she says.
"However, I ask that at this time, Counter Terrorism Policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.â
In the update, CTP adds that the five suspects - who are all UK nationals - are being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace).
The investigation into establishing "circumstances of the activity of those arrested, their knowledge and any motivation behind this incident" remains ongoing, the force says.
Counter Terrorism Policing Senior National Coordinator, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans says: "This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the MoD, and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community.
"I know this has been incredibly disruptive for local people, but Iâd like to reassure them that our activity is in the interest of national security, but most importantly in the interest of their own safety."
We've just received an update from Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) on yesterday's incident at RAF Fairford.
CTP says the five people arrested are all male in their early to mid-20s. All five are UK nationals from London.

this platform,â he says.

"The prime minister at the time, Keir Starmer, then partially
relented and said, 'Well OK, you can use them for defensive purposes, you can use
our bases to hit Iranian missile and drone sites that are attacking our Gulf
allies but thatâs all. We donât want them used to bomb targets further inside
Iran'.
"But in July, Iran said anybody who allows their bases to be
used to attack us will make themselves a target," he says.

behind this, rather than say, Russia or jihadists."

articles.title_orig: China and the U.S. Pledge to Cut Tariffs on $60 Billion in Goods
articles.title_zh: China and the U.S. Pledge to Cut Tariffs on $60 Billion in Goods
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The U.S. and China are planning to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, according to government announcements from both sides Monday.
The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.
Cooke, whose company primarily helps U.S. brands sell in China, said that Beijing's import list includes fast-growing categories such as hair care and packaged pet food, where Chinese brands are highly competitive against U.S. offerings. "Every percentage point counts for price competitiveness and preserving margin."
However, it was not immediately clear when lower tariffs would take effect, and by how much the duties would go down. The U.S. and China last year slapped import tariffs effectively of over 40% and more than 30%, respectively, on each other.
The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides said the highly anticipated U.S.-China "Board of Trade" would consist of officials from both governments, and would meet at least once a quarter , with the top officials meeting "whenever necessary."
Lower tariffs could substantially boost trade, especially for highly competitive Chinese companies. Home goods seller Ryan Zhao, director of Jiangsu Green Willow Textile, expects sales in the second half of the year to grow by 30% from a year ago if tariff cuts are implemented.
Here's a select list of products set to benefit:
Plates, cups, bowls, serving dishes
Blankets (including electric ones) and rugs
Christmas-tree lamps and ornaments
Toys (including tricycles, but excluding items that connect to WiFi or Bluetooth)
Billiards balls, chalk and tables
Rackets for games, other than for "lawn-tennis or badminton"
Soccer balls, baseballs, softballs, lawn-tennis balls
Fish hooks and fishing line
Horses, donkeys, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, chickens for breeding
Frozen, fresh or chilled whole chickens or turkeys
Rabbit meat, excluding rabbit heads
Dried, smoked or salted beef
Live freshwater ornamental fish
Ice cream and other frozen products
—CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

Morning Rundown: U.S. Marines injured in undisclosed Iranian attack, the MAGA push to derail last Jan. 6 prosecution, and Taylor Swift sets VMAs record
LOS ANGELES — The MTV Video Music Awards made their West Coast return Sunday. But like many Angelenos when they get stuck in traffic, the show was fashionably late when it aired on CBS.
A football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Dallas Cowboys ran long, delaying the telecast by about 20 minutes . Many viewers complained that attendees and news outlets that were at the Peacock Theater were spoiling the roughly two-hour show by posting live updates on social media.
But the show went on after the telecast hiccup, with host Snoop Dogg keeping it running in a timely manner.
The rapper, a 13-time VMAs nominee and three-time winner, promised viewers that the awards would be “the biggest party the VMAs has ever seen.”
Here are some of the night’s biggest moments.
Madonna, 68, returned to the VMAs for the first time in 23 years to open the show, with help from Sabrina Carpenter and Charli XCX.
“It’s mother,” she announced as she graced the stage.
Carpenter reunited with the star to perform their dance track, “Bring Your Love,” which they debuted at Coachella in April during Carpenter’s headlining set.
“Brat” artist Charli XCX and Madonna also performed their single, “Danceteria Afterhours.” Their performance featured a slew of cameos, including actors Julia Fox, Julia Garner, Debi Mazar and Seth Rogen; record producer and songwriter Andrew Watt; fashion designer Tony Ward; and visual artist Fab 5 Freddie.
Madonna was nominated in 13 categories this year, the most of any nominee, for her album “Confessions II.” She took home three awards, including artist of the year.
During her last VMAs appearance, in 2003, she made headlines for kissing both Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera onstage, a controversial and iconic moment that made pop culture history.
Accepting the artist of the year statue, she reflected on her performance at the first VMAs 43 years ago, when, she said, her then-manager told her that her career “was over” after she experienced a wardrobe malfunction onstage.
“Seriously, I really want you to know that I spent the last year and a half finding myself, believing in myself and really making the music that I wanted to make,” Madonna said. “And to me, that really is the definition of being an artist. And my hope for all of you here tonight is that you spend the next year or the next 10 years or the rest of your life doing the same, finding yourself and believing in yourself.”
The death of Dolly Parton , known as the big-hearted “Queen of Country,” rattled the world last month, with tributes pouring in from fans across cultural, political, geographic and generational lines.
So it came as no surprise when the VMAs decided to honor the Hollywood legend, who died at age 80 after a brief battle with cancer.
Grammy winner Kacey Musgraves, best known for her “Golden Hour” album, paid homage to Parton on Sunday. She performed Parton’s hit “I Will Always Love You.” Footage of Parton appeared before Musgraves performed.
Taylor Swift later dedicated her award to Parton, calling her the “original showgirl.”
Later in the night, the VMAs also remembered pop superstar and Wham! band member George Michael, who died in 2016 at age 53.
The tribute featured performances from: Sombr, who sang “Faith” and “Father Figure”; Raye, who sang “I Knew You Were Waiting (For Me)”; Teddy Swims, who sang “Careless Whisper”; and Adam Lambert, who closed the set with “Freedom! ’90.”
The VMAs never shies away from nostalgia. And this year was no different, with the awards show honoring Nirvana with its coveted Video Vanguard Award.
Surviving Nirvana members Dave Grohl, Krist Novoselic and Pat Smear reunited to accept the award.
The rock group’s last appearance together at the VMAs was in 1994, five months after frontman Kurt Cobain died.
“Nirvana continues to resonate so deeply because people are still hungry for authenticity,” Novoselic said onstage. “For something real, something uncompromising, something that tells you it’s just OK to come as you are.”
Getting married to NFL star Travis Kelce in July was not the only milestone for Swift this year.
On Sunday, she surpassed Beyoncé to become the most-awarded artist in VMAs history when she brought her Moon Person statue total to 32. Swift and Beyoncé had been tied with 30 VMAs.
The VMAs honored Swift with its inaugural Artist Director Honors , which organizers said was designed to celebrate someone “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling.”
Swift’s friend Dakota Johnson, the actor, described her as a “visionary” before she presented her with the award.
Taylor Swift becomes VMAs' first Artist Director honoree
“I got to start making music videos and being part of music videos 20 years ago, and since then I’ve gotten to be a part of making 60 music videos,” Swift said as she accepted the Moon Person onstage. “Eighteen of those I wrote and directed, and I really love writing and directing music videos. The main reason ... is because you, the fans, make it so much fun, you make it so rewarding, because you actually care about what we’re making.”
She thanked MTV and her fans before she debuted the music video for her song “Patient Zero,” which stars Johnson and Colin Farrell and was directed by Swift. Oscar winner Emmanuel Lubezki, known for “The Revenant” and “Birdman,” did cinematography for the video.
Swift surprised her fans last week by releasing brand-new bonus tracks from the “Showgirl” album, which she wrote and produced in Sweden with Max Martin and Shellback. In addition to “Patient Zero,” “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” tracks include “Cleveland!” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon.”
Swift was nominated in 11 categories Sunday for her “The Life of a Showgirl” album , which was released almost one year ago.
Saba Hamedy is the trends and culture editor for NBC News.

Ted Kaczynski was 16 when he entered Harvard University as a mathematics prodigy. Years later, he would become known as the Unabomber, after carrying out a bombing campaign that killed three people and injured 23 others between 1978 and 1995.
Netflix’s Unabomber directed by Janus Metz, explores Kaczynski’s life before and during the events that led to his capture. Jacob Tremblay plays the younger Kaczynski, while Russell Crowe portrays Harvard professor Henry Murray, Shailene Woodley plays FBI agent Joanne Miller and Annabelle Wallis portrays Christiana Morgan, Murray’s academic collaborator.
“We decided to explore Ted Kaczynski's time at Harvard, as it stood out as a formative and fragile period in his life,” Metz tells TIME. “We wanted to understand who this young man was up until he began his descent into a darker and deadlier path.”
Born in Chicago in 1942, Kaczynski demonstrated exceptional mathematical ability from an early age. He entered Harvard at 16 before continuing his studies at the University of Michigan, where he earned a master’s degree and a doctorate in mathematics.
At 25, he became a professor at the University of California, Berkeley. But he left the university in 1969 and eventually moved to a remote cabin near Lincoln, Mont., where he lived without electricity or running water.
Kaczynski became increasingly isolated from society. He spent much of his time reading, hunting and growing plants, while developing increasingly strong opposition to modern technology and industrial society.
In 1978, Kaczynski began the bombing campaign that would eventually span nearly two decades. His first known attack involved a homemade device mailed to a professor at Northwestern University. It exploded when opened by a campus security officer, causing minor injuries. In November 1979, Kaczynski placed a device aboard an American Airlines flight, causing smoke inhalation injuries and forcing the plane to make an emergency landing.
Over the years, his targets included universities, airlines and people he associated with technology and the modern industrial system.
The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM, short for “University and Airline Bombing,” before Kaczynski’s identity was known. The media later used it to name him the “Unabomber.” Between 1978 and 1995, 16 attacks were linked to the case, killing Hugh Scrutton, Thomas Mosser and Gilbert Murray and injuring 23 people.
Kaczynski’s identity remained a mystery for years. That changed in 1995, when he sent a lengthy manifesto titled “Industrial Society and Its Future”  to The Washington Post and The New York Times and demanded that it be published. The approximately 35,000-word text laid out his opposition to modern technological society and explored ideas about human freedom, autonomy, and the effects of industrialization.
The FBI supported the decision to publish the manifesto in the hope that someone familiar with Kaczynski’s writing would recognize it. That person turned out to be his brother David’s wife, Linda Patrik.
After reading the manifesto, Patrik noticed similarities between its ideas and the writing she had previously seen from Kaczynski. She brought her concerns to David, who initially struggled to believe that his brother could be responsible for the attacks.
David eventually examined the manifesto alongside an essay Kaczynski had written years earlier. The similarities in their language and ideas were striking enough for him to contact the FBI.
The material gave investigators a crucial lead. After years of attacks and an extensive investigation, Kaczynski was now directly connected to the manifesto and the writings that could help identify him as the person behind the Unabomber case.
Shailene Woodley in Unabomber Courtesy of Netflix
On April 3, 1996, nearly two decades after the first attack, federal agents surrounded Kaczynski’s remote cabin near Lincoln, Mont., and arrested him.
The search of the property gave investigators a trove of evidence. Inside, they found bomb-making materials, a typewriter, coded diary entries and approximately 40,000 pages of handwritten notes, along with a completed bomb.
Kaczynski later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in prison without parole. He remained incarcerated until his death in 2023 at age 81.
While in prison, Kaczynski was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia by a psychiatrist who interviewed him. He rejected the idea that he was mentally incapable of understanding his actions. In a 1999 interview with TIME , he said he was certain he was sane.
While at Harvard, Kaczynski took part in psychological experiments overseen by professor Henry Murray. Murray worked with Christiana Morgan at the Harvard Psychological Clinic, where they developed the Thematic Apperception Test, or TAT.
“Christiana was the co-creator of the Harvard school of psychology where the tests on Ted Kaczynski took place,” says Wallis, who plays Morgan in the movie. “Murray and Morgan were collaborators at the time and together devised the highly controversial stress tests used on Harvard students. I was fascinated to learn about the extent of her involvement.”
The experiments involved students writing about their beliefs before undergoing intense psychological sessions. They later became an important part of discussions about Kaczynski’s life, although their precise impact on him remains uncertain.
The full Harvard file on Kaczynski remains classified, making it impossible to know exactly what Murray concluded from the experiments.
“I don't think the Murray experiments in themselves turned Ted Kaczynski into the Unabomber,” says Metz. “There are many factors in Ted Kaczynski's life that contributed to his evolution.”
However, Metz says the experiments were designed to break down participants who knew very little about what they were being subjected to, and that the filmmakers wanted to show them as “likely a piece of the puzzle.”
Metz also points to Kaczynski’s own writings as another part of the story.
“We also know from Ted Kaczynski's own journals that he wanted revenge from feeling disrespected and rejected, which these experiments could have contributed to,” he says.
According to Metz, Kaczynski himself later claimed that the experiments had not had a significant effect on him.
Russell Crowe and Jacob Tremblay in Unabomber Courtesy of Netflix
For Tremblay, one of the challenges of playing Kaczynski was the lack of detailed information about his early life.
“While there is plenty of information to go off of from Ted's adult life, it was challenging to find material regarding his early life when I played him,” Tremblay says. “I was left with a rather blank canvas in terms of how much freedom I would have with the character.”
Tremblay listened to recordings of Kaczynski’s interrogation after his arrest to study his speech patterns and watched footage of him as an adult, noting his stiff posture. I then put my own youthful, nervous and softer spin on that,” Tremblay says.
The psychological experiment scenes presented a different challenge. Tremblay was strapped to a chair, limiting his movement and expressions. “I learned to utilize that unfamiliar and uncomfortable environment to my advantage,” Tremblay says. “Because Ted himself in that moment is also experiencing that discomfort and unfamiliarity at the same time.”
Unabomber is grounded in documented events from Kaczynski’s life, but the film also takes creative liberties with gaps in the historical record.

articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says Trump must choose between war or diplomacy as talks expected to resume this week
articles.content_orig:
Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over U.S. sanctions against its aviation sector, which have forced the cancellation of many flights across the region, state media reported Monday.
The U.S. imposed restrictions this month on the entire Iranian aviation industry and vowed to take a hard line against any companies or countries that continue to assist it.
As the sanctions took effect last Wednesday, some major airlines were forced to cancel international flights as several nations in the region implemented bans.
"To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)," said civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.
In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah - who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began - said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."
He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.
U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.
The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.
Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.
The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.
Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.
Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center .
Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Since the outbreak of the war in February, negotiations between Tehran and Washington have occurred largely through mediators.
U.K. police said five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran were being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
RAF Fairford, a U.K. Royal Air Force base about 85 miles west of London in rural Gloucestershire, has been used by American bombers to conduct strikes against Iranian missile sites. The British government, under an agreement made under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, granted the U.S. permission to use Farford and other key U.K. bases provided it was only for strikes defined as defensive in nature.
Authorities are investigating a link between the arrests in Fairford and Iran as one possibility. Iranian authorities have declared all bases used to attack Iranian territory as legitimate targets.
President Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests.
"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.
"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."
"At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.
President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.
Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.
President Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after he rejected a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to the U.S. to reopen the Strait of Hormuz over seven days, but Mr. Trump asserted that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly."
"They overplayed their hand," Mr. Trump told Axios.
The president said resuming strikes on Iran was not off the table, adding: "I am always thinking about it."
epublican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said Iran's proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks was "not a serious offer."
"The president's not Bambi's baby brother. He turned it down," Kennedy said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"We need to continue doing what we're doing — the sanctions, the blockade," said Kennedy.
"Now there's just one problem: The strait is at least partially closed, and it's affected the price of oil. And oil's in everything, including gasoline, and it's painful as hell," he said, adding: "We've got to either figure out a way to settle this thing, to get the strait open, or to escalate."
Kennedy said he would not support sending U.S. ground troops into Iran, however.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
articles.title_zh: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.
The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
Tune in at 8 a.m. ET as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to CNBC about this news. Watch in real time on CNBC+ or the CNBC Pro stream.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July. That's when OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached Hugging Face, which operates an open-source developer platform.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company. "From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers. But CEO Jensen Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
"You have to think about what you could have done, what's the solution for it,"  Huang said in a podcast with The New York Times' Ezra Klein released last week, referring to recent incidents. "In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off an industry firestorm two weeks ago, urging AI model developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of the models spinning out of control, an argument that was supported by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk .
Nvidia's new offering is an engineering solution to the agent safety issue, Boitano said.
"Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do," Boitano said.
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities. Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners. Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the $810 million in spending canceled by President Trump
articles.title_zh: What to know about the $810 million in spending canceled by President Trump
articles.content_orig:
Democrats are blaming Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought for the canceled funds, accusing him of violating the separation of powers and undermining Congressional authority. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images North America hide caption
Each year, Congress passes laws which allocate money to the federal government's various programs and agencies. Trump, for the second year in a row, is refusing to send some of that money to the places that Congress says it has to go , setting off a fresh battle with lawmakers over who controls federal spending.
Of the $810 million being withheld, $567 million comes from programs that "provided services to refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens," according to a memo from the White House.
The move, called a pocket rescission, is illegal, according to the Government Accountability Office , an independent, non-partisan watchdog agency charged with providing federal agencies fact-based information.
Article 1 of the Constitution gives Congress t he power to levy taxes and decide how federal funds are spent — known as power of the purse. If the president disagrees, he or she can send a request to Congress to cancel the fund, but that is supposed to happen with 45 days notice in order to let Congress agree or disagree.
A pocket rescission happens when the president decides to cancel funds without ample time for Congress to weigh in or reallocate the money. With the end of the fiscal year less than a week away, the announcement means the funds will go unspent and Congress can't respond.
"This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress's Constitutional power of the purse," Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations committee, wrote in a statement posted to X. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."
The canceled funds are fueling anger from Democrats who say OMB director Russell Vought is violating the separation of powers and undermining Congressional authority.
"This is theft from the American people, plain and simple," wrote Washington Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee on X. "Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because Vought is saying their votes don't count."
"Donald Trump knows he can't get these cuts through Congress, so he is illegally making them through the back door," Rep. Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget committee, said in a statement. "Trump's actions are a blatant attack on Congress's constitutional power of the purse."
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
The administration also says it withheld $15 million to a Justice Department team tasked with "preventing and resolving racial and ethnic tensions, incidents, and civil disorders, and in restoring racial stability and harmony," $70 million to "programs provide grants and fellowships to support institutions bringing foreign students and faculty to the United States to study or teach language," and tens of millions to various research and non-profit grant programs that target climate change or racial and gender minority work.
A detailed accounting provided by the administration can be found here .

articles.title_orig: Trump asked China’s president if he wants to buy US arms, ambassador says
articles.title_zh: Trump asked China’s president if he wants to buy US arms, ambassador says
articles.content_orig:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island
Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”
On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington .
The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn (£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal was announced in December last year.
Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned . At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.
Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.
Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.
After Perdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times the US had no plans to sell arms to China , while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
China is a net exporter of weapons. Of the arms that it does import, most come from Russia, but the volume is rapidly falling thanks to advances in China’s own military manufacturing capacity. China’s arms imports fell by 72% between 2021 and 2025 compared with the previous five years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Before the interview, the Taiwanese deputy foreign minister, Chen Ming-chi, spoke of the severe military threat China posed.
“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.
On Sunday, a Taiwanese official, Shen Yu-chung, also pushed back on what he said was an attempt by Beijing to “falsely claim that the Chinese Communist party and the US were allies” in the second world war. A fact sheet released by the White House after the Trump-Xi summit had said China and the US “fought side by side to win” in the war.
China’s government during the second world war was the Republic of China led by Chiang Kai-shek. Chiang’s government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, who established the People’s Republic of China in 1949.
In recent years Taiwan has sought to emphasise its history of fighting alongside western democratic allies as it hopes to bolster international support against aggression from Beijing.
Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.
Perdue told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Goldman Warns Diesel Export Ban Would Send Gasoline Prices Higher
articles.title_zh: Goldman Warns Diesel Export Ban Would Send Gasoline Prices Higher
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested the White House is still considering a diesel export ban as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle soaring fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November .
"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump told a Fox News reporter on Sunday, while attending the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Illinois.
"That can oftentimes lead to a little bit of an increase on gasoline for cars, so we're looking at it very seriously. We may do it," he added.
Trump has previously indicated support for an export ban as retail diesel prices have climbed to fresh record highs, saying earlier this month that a decision would be made quickly " one way or another " on whether to implement a ban.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said the White House is considering restrictions rather than an outright ban, while Politico reported last week that the Trump administration was preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days.
The idea of the world's largest diesel exporter implementing an outright ban has prompted firm pushback from the U.S. energy industry, while analysts have warned that the move could backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis.
Diesel prices have soared amid hostilities between the U.S. and Iran , as well as Russia and Ukraine , with the conflicts disrupting vital oil and fuel trade routes. Average U.S. diesel prices hovered around $6.50 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA , up sharply from a year ago but just below their record high of $6.53 on Sept. 22.
Commodity strategists at Morgan Stanley have said an export restriction from the U.S., which has become an important source of marginal diesel supply amid reduced flow from Russia and the Middle East, would likely lower U.S. diesel prices initially — "but with potentially adverse reactions downstream."
"Not only would diesel prices be higher globally, but there could be a feedback loop to US gasoline prices as refinery runs adjust," strategists at Morgan Stanley said in a research note published Thursday.
Benedict George, head of European product pricing at Argus Media, said some form of U.S. restriction on diesel exports would likely send European diesel prices and premiums against crude "to a new unprecedented level," noting that the U.S. has supplied about half of Europe's diesel imports over the last couple of months.
"It's really important to be clear that there is no measure yet and it's very unclear whether there will be a measure at all and what the measure will be even if there is a vision," George told CNBC by telephone.
When talking to oil traders in Europe, it's clear that they mostly doubt the U.S. is going to restrict diesel exports, given how challenging a move would be for U.S. oil companies, George said.
In the U.S., soaring diesel prices have put additional financial strain on farmers and agricultural workers, as well as drivers and households ahead of the November midterm elections.
The American Petroleum Institute (API), an oil lobby group, was among those to have quickly contested the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban when Trump initially appeared to back the idea last week.
In a statement , API CEO Mike Sommers said that "restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers."
He added: "The answer is more supply and more flexibility—not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse."
Trump has previously urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices.
Ukraine, which fears an extremely difficult winter period amid expectations of another Russian assault on its energy infrastructure, has previously characterized Russian oil refineries as legitimate military targets.
Argus' George said Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries have added a whole new layer to the global supply crunch, making diesel "the biggest problem for the global oil system, whereas before it was one of several very big problems."
Asked for his outlook on how long the global diesel supply crunch could last, George said the uncertainty is so extreme that some traders have simply given up trying to forecast the market.
"One trader was saying to me recently that he doesn't bother trying to forecast now because it feels like a waste of effort. You have literally no idea what is going to happen," George said.
"We don't know if the U.S. will introduce any restrictions, but I think all anybody has talked about is a short-term measure, so two or three months at an absolute most … so there is a kind of time horizon on the U.S. restriction of exports, if it were to happen," he continued.
"But on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, who knows? I mean, literally nobody knows. Nothing has worked so far to resolve that situation and similarly for the semi-closure of the Strait of Hormuz."
— CNBC's Spencer Kimball & Michael Bloom contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Powerful nor’easter floods Northeast again, causing problems from New Jersey to New England
articles.title_zh: Powerful nor’easter floods Northeast again, causing problems from New Jersey to New England
articles.content_orig:
Powerful weather system pummels shoreline for a second day, knocking out power to tens of thousands
Residents of coastal communities in the US’s north-east slogged through floodwaters for a second day as a powerful storm known as a nor’easter pummeled the shoreline on Sunday , knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes.
Tidal surges swamped low-lying neighborhoods in New Jersey while wind gusts toppled trees on New York ’s Long Island, damaging homes and bringing down utility poles.
In the New Jersey beach town of Sea Bright, each high tide brought a new round of flooding. “It’s not like a one-time occurrence,” said Caroline Virenius, whose garage filled with about a foot of water (30cm). “It’s getting wet again and again.”
The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City Housing Authority worker when a tree fell on Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf all the way to New England.
Extreme amounts of rain – more than 4 inches (10cm) since Friday in some spots in New Jersey – combined with a surging ocean led to flooding amounts not seen for close to a decade in places used to dealing with high water, residents said.
The National Weather Service (NWS) predicted the storm would weaken over Sunday night with local heavy rain in parts of New England and the mid-Atlantic. But local officials in New Jersey and New York told residents that high tide late on Monday could bring more flooding.
“There is another band of the storm, a weaker band, but still another band that could hit early this afternoon and later into the evening,” said New York’s Nassau county executive, Bruce Blakeman.
The nor’easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy , which left behind over $60bn in damage across the eastern US in 2012. While this storm’s impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the east coast during the fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that is disrupting this year’s weather.
Images of waves crashing into sea walls and on to beaches raised concerns about coastal erosion.
Well over 100,000 customers were without power across the north-east and mid-Atlantic at times on Sunday, according to PowerOutage.us . The most widespread outages were in counties along the coast from New Jersey to Connecticut.
The total number of outages across the US had fallen on Monday morning to about 55,000, with more than 10,000 of those reported in Hawaii, which was dealing with the threat of heavy, flash flooding and strong winds as Hurricane Nolo moved away from the state.
Numerous flights were canceled or delayed up and down the east coast. More than 250 flights had been canceled at Boston Logan international airport by late Sunday morning as wind gusts reached 40mph (64km/h), according to the Massachusetts Port Authority.
The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected on Sunday from northern New Jersey into southern New England.
While the storm was gradually weakening, tidal flooding would stay through high-tide cycles on Sunday night, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service (NWS) in College Park, Maryland.
In New York City, water a few inches deep filled streets in the Howard Beach neighborhood but did not deter residents from venturing out for coffee on Sunday morning.
Carole Ann Palmer, who owns Jingles Bait and Tackle in North Beach Haven, New Jersey, said this was the worst flooding she had seen in 10 years.
“Yesterday, I was like, oh my God, it just keeps getting higher and higher,” said Palmer, who lives above the store.
The front step was swept away in the storm, and she saw neighbors kayaking through the streets on Saturday.
Her biggest problem on Sunday was taking her two puppies outside to relieve themselves. She had to put on waders and carry them to dry land.
“I take one at the time, carry them across the street so they can do their business and then come back, dry them off and then do the other one. It’s a workout,” Palmer said.
Bernard Dowd waded through tidal water on Sunday to get to his Sea Bright home, a day after he got back from work to find his basement “filled up like a swimming pool”.
But he said the situation around his neighborhood would probably have been much worse if it were not for new rules requiring homeowners to raise the height of their homes in the wake of Sandy, which devastated the community.
He also noticed that many around the community had lined their homes and businesses with sandbags – something he wishes he had done too.
“I’m always thinking they are hyping the storm,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks protests in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.title_zh: Eviction of 87-year-old sparks protests in Madrid over housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
Protesters camp during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen to demand stronger laws to protect renters at Sol square in Madrid, Spain, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. Manu Fernandez/AP hide caption
MADRID — Protesters outraged by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman camped overnight in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza, where more demonstrators — including multigenerational families — joined them on Sunday for a second day of protests over Spain's housing crisis.
Tens of thousands marched through Madrid on Saturday to protest the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal from the apartment in the upscale Retiro neighborhood where she had lived for more than seven decades.
The demonstrators are demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable.
Many refused to leave after Saturday's march and pitched tents in Puerta del Sol for the night.
"The housing situation is unsustainable," said Natalia Navarro, a 27-year-old actress who was among those camping out at the plaza. "We are all out on the street because we are fed up."
"The wave of indignation and anger that has been unleashed is now unstoppable," said Alicia del Río, a spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union, which led the protests.
"We will remain here" until the government passes new laws, including indefinite rental contracts, and stops evictions like Abascal's, del Río told journalists at the plaza on Sunday. Spain's Socialist-led government is expected to announce new measures in its weekly cabinet meeting next Tuesday.
Protesters camp during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen to demand stronger laws to protect renters at Sol square in Madrid, Spain, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. Manu Fernandez/AP hide caption
On Sept. 23, Abascal was carried from her apartment on a stretcher and placed in an ambulance as supporters — who had tried unsuccessfully to stop the eviction — chanted her nickname, "Maricarmen."
"I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," Abascal said in a video recorded from her hospital bed after the eviction.
Images of the eviction spread widely across Spain, fueling outrage and criticism of public authorities and real estate investment companies accused of pricing residents out of their homes. Critics often refer to such companies as "vulture funds."
"Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest," said Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher who took part in Saturday's protests.
Speaking at a Socialist Party rally in Madrid, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez addressed Abascal directly: "I have a message for you, Maricarmen: the government is working around the clock to bring a Royal Decree on housing next Tuesday. And I ask parliamentary groups to make one last effort to have it validated in the National Parliament for Maricarmen."
Abascal has criticized Sánchez and blamed him for her ordeal.
"Does he not realize the quantity of evictions that there are daily?" she asked during an interview with Spain's state broadcaster RTVE the day before she was forcibly removed from her home. "Does he not realize, or does he not want to realize?"
Maricarmen, 87, waits at home for police to arrive before being evicted from the home where she lived in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press via AP hide caption
Spanish media reported that Abascal's father first rented the apartment in 1956 and that she remained there as a tenant under rent controls after her parents died.
The building changed ownership in 2018, and Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants' Union.
Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($570) to 2,650 euros.
It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros, which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.
Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market, despite strong economic growth in Europe's fourth-largest economy. Incomes have not kept pace with the rising housing costs, and analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply.
The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share.
The demonstrations in the symbolic Madrid plaza this weekend reminded many in Spain of the historic demonstrations starting May 15, 2011, when members of the "indignados movement" camped for 28 days straight, sparking similar sit-ins across the country and the world. That movement was a reaction to evictions and other issues following a global economic crisis, including unemployment, austerity measures and corruption.
Estefania Molina, a political scientist and columnist, said the stakes of popular frustration are growing. In 2011, "people protested because they couldn't buy an apartment."
"Today, the protest is about not being able to rent a room in someone else's home," she told Spanish television.
Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for subsidized public rental housing, which represents less than 2% of the country's housing stock. The European Union average is 8%.

articles.title_orig: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 28 dead
articles.title_zh: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 28 dead
articles.content_orig:
Twenty-eight people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.
Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 14 more injured.
In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.
South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks.
In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.
Police said only four of those killed have been identified so far.
Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African.
He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups.
Mining without permission in abandoned shafts or dump sites is a persistent problem in South Africa, causing numerous deaths from unsafe conditions. Authorities say the miners are typically undocumented migrants recruited by organised crime gangs.
Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP.
He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.
In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.
No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.
The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.
Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million.
But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence.
On Saturday, a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni , to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths.

articles.title_orig: AEW wrestling star Benjamin Satterley, known as Pac, dies at 40
articles.title_zh: AEW wrestling star Benjamin Satterley, known as Pac, dies at 40
articles.content_orig:
Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star known by his ring name Pac, has died at 40, according to All Elite Wrestling.
“A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability,” said AEW in its announcement Sunday night.
“Pac signed with All Elite Wrestling in 2019 and held multiple AEW Championships and competed in some of the most memorable matches in AEW history,” it said, extending condolences to his family, friends and fans.
He previously wrestled for WWE under the ring name Neville, and became known for his aerial attacks and explosive style – earning himself nicknames like “King of the Cruiserweights” and “The Man That Gravity Forgot.”
The circumstances and cause of his death were not provided.
The announcement came just a day after Satterley wrestled a match at AEW’s “All Out” pay-per-view event near Chicago, going up against Andrade El Ídolo.
During his acclaimed career, Satterley made history as the inaugural AEW All-Atlantic Champion in 2022 before the title changed to the AEW International Championship. He was also an acclaimed AEW World Trios Champion, winning the championship alongside teammates Claudio Castagnoli and Wheeler Yuta in front of tens of thousands of fans at Wembley Stadium in his home country in 2024.
Satterley’s death comes just a few weeks after another AEW wrestler, Andy Williams, known professionally as The Butcher, died after collapsing at an independent match in Pennsylvania, according to AEW. He was 48.
Tributes for Satterley have poured in from fans and peers in the wrestling world.
Fellow AEW wrestler Nick Wayne, the youngest champion in AEW history, recalled speaking with Satterley in 2024 after watching him in a match. Satterley’s “conversations, advice, and positive thoughts going into things is something I always cherished,” Wayne wrote on X . “PAC is one of the greatest innovators and Professional Wrestlers to ever do it.”
Will Ospreay, also an English wrestler signed with AEW, who has faced Satterley many times in the ring, posted on X that Satterley was “the greatest export from our country. Also the greatest human being.”
Since joining AEW in 2019, Satterley had wrestled in 147 matches, with 94 wins, 47 losses, and four draws, according to the AEW website.
He also wrestled for Japanese promotions Dragongate and New Japan Pro-Wrestling, as well as the Consejo Mundial de Lucha Libre. After the news of his death, New Japan said it was “deeply saddened” by his passing, expressing its sympathies for his friends and family.
CMLL also expressed its condolences, writing on X it will “remember his extraordinary professionalism, dedication, and respect in every appearance in Mexico.”

articles.title_orig: Bo Nix and Talanoa Hufanga lead the Broncos past the Rams 30-26 in a Sunday night thriller
articles.title_zh: Bo Nix and Talanoa Hufanga lead the Broncos past the Rams 30-26 in a Sunday night thriller
articles.content_orig:
The Denver Broncos secured a famous 30-26 win over the LA Rams , in what was another spectacular second-half performance from Bo Nix .
He threw an interception in the first half and was largely disappointing as the Broncos went scoreless. The Rams looked poised to secure another win, but the Broncos showed great resilience in the second half.
Led by their quarterback Bo Nix, they scored 16 points in the third quarter to make it an interesting fourth quarter.
With 3:38 left, Matthew Stafford threw a 48-yard touchdown pass to Konta Mumpfield to give the Rams a 26-23 lead, but it was then followed by a thrilling TD from Nix with just 47 seconds left to play.
This was Nix's 10th fourth-quarter comeback win since coming into the league, the most for any QB in the league.
Bo Nix has been one of the best young quarterbacks in the league, but like every other young QB, he has a few things to work on.
For the former Oregon QB, it definitely has to be consistent in throwing the ball.
However, journalist Tim Hasselbeck admires one quality Nix has that makes him special.
"What I like is, when you see him [Bo Nix] on the sidelines, there's a smile, he seems unfazed with the idea that the offense is struggling, that is a great trait to have as a quarterback to not appear to be bothered whether he is not, maybe he isn't bothered by it at all, which allows him to play well as the game continues to go along," said Hasselbeck on SportsCenter.
Coach Sean Payton was happy with how Nix finished the game, but had serious questions about the first-half performance.
"The moments aren't too big and he [Bo Nix] moves and escapes and makes plays, but it leads us to the first part of the jigsaw which is, man, we have to find a way to play better earlier," Payton said in his press conference.
Fans in Denver were not too pleased with how the first half ended. However, Nix inspired his teammates to force a comeback against what many believe are going to be contenders to win the Super Bowl.
The Broncos will be up against the San Francisco 49ers next week. Keion White and Fred Warner will be the players waiting for Nix there, which is going to be a tough test for the young QB.

articles.title_orig: Taylor Swift Premieres Star-Filled 'Patient Zero' Music Video at VMAs
articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift Premieres Star-Filled 'Patient Zero' Music Video at VMAs
articles.content_orig:
Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic
It’s a love story? Hardly — it’s a ghost story. Taylor Swift brought her “ Patient Zero ” music video to the MTV Video Music Awards Sunday night for its official world premiere, following up the release of the single at the beginning of the weekend with visuals that take the triangle in the song into more dramatic and even spookier realms than might have been anticipated. Dakota Johnson and Colin Ferrell amping up the tension, which ultimately has reverberations that go beyond just a bad breakup.
Fans had only seen a 13-second teaser for the video prior to its premiere on the CBS/MTV/Paramount+ telecast, and they now know which character the headstone was for in the cemetery Swift and Johnson visit.
The video is, of course, Swift’s latest directorial effort, and the occasion of her attendance at the VMAs was receiving the inaugural Artist-Director Honor. It was not her only trip to the podium; after the initial speech and video premiere, Swift came back later in the show to accept a video of the year award for “The Fate of Ophelia,” at which point she thanked Dolly Parton for her inspiration.
The singer’s initial remarks prior to sharing the video were brief, after an introduction by Johnson. “First of all, I want to say thank you to MTV for giving this platform to music videos so long ago,” Swift began. “I got to start making music videos and being a part of music videos 20 years ago, and since then, I’ve gotten to be a part of making 60 music videos — roughly 60. Eighteen of those, I wrote and directed, and I really love writing and directing music videos. I’ve gotta tell you, though, that the main reason why I love writing and directing music videos so much is because you, the fans, make it so much fun. It’s so rewarding because you actually care about what we’re making. So, you know, I wanna say thank you to everyone who ever worked on a music video that I got to be a part of. I learned something from every single person that ever worked alongside me on these projects. Mainly I want to say thank you to the fans…
“And rather than say anything else, I think rather than than keep talking, I would love to, if it’s OK with you, show you my latest music video, stsarring my friend Dakota Johnson and Colin Ferrell. Cinematography by Chivo.”
“Chivo” is a nickname for Oscar-winning cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, who often works with Steven Spielberg, and who was shooting a Swift video for the first time. She seems especially enamored of that collaboration; Lubezki’s name came up as the first and only onscreen credit at the end of the premiere.
The video has Johnson and Farrell portraying a couple whose relationship appears on the rocks, with Swift acting as a counselor to the woman, singing lyrics about how she is the man’s ex and can tell her exactly how things will go. Things are just a little less sinister in the song’s lyrics than in the way things play out on screen. Johnson is seen getting angry with Johnson after a banquet at which he speaks, as the music drops out for a driving scene in which he seems to be gaslighting her with accusations about her drinking, after she has become upset at the sight of him flirting with female guests.
The video cuts to flashback of similar experiences in which Swift, his then-companion, reacted more angrily to his infractions. There’s a headline that reads “Heiress dies of mystery illness — husband inherits billions” (with the additional explanation, “Spouse inherits estate amid unanswered questions”). Then we see the two women standing at a gravestone with a photo that suggests it was Swift’s character who was born in 1986 and died in 2022. Johnson places black roses on the headstone of Swift’s dead heiress character, with it left unclear whether she’s taken any lessons from Swift’s purely spectral counsel or not.
The Patient Zero video is finally out in the world! Getting to work with Emmanuel Lubezki was something out of a dream sequence, and I learned so much from getting to watch his genius in action. I want to thank Dakota and Colin for trusting me with their time, taste, and talent… pic.twitter.com/vkLCO167Ea
Swift was more expansive in her remarks about the new video in a message she posted on social media immediately after the premiere. “The ‘Patient Zero’ video is finally out in the world!” she wrote. “Getting to work with Emmanuel Lubezki was something out of a dream sequence, and I learned so much from getting to watch his genius in action. I want to thank Dakota and Colin for trusting me with their time, taste, and talent (giggling with your friend because you’re twinning for an entire shoot was a new and truly delightful experience). And Colin’s turn as a villain is even more impressive when you get to be around him. He’s an absolute light and as kind as they come. Cara, thank you for agreeing to play the lusty other woman. That’s what friends are for? With the ‘Patient Zero’ video, I got to explore the cinematic and literary genres I love so much. I wanted to incorporate elements of gothic ghost stories, true crime, psychological thrillers all in a setting I hadn’t really shot in much. The house was a metaphor for the coldness of a relationship that’s faded and atrophied. Thank you to Ethan Tobman for your insightful production design, and bringing that feeling to life. My editor Chancler Haynes has outdone himself. And lastly, thank you to the VMAs for giving us a World Premiere at the place where celebrating music videos became a thing. And so much love for you guys, always.”
Following the VMAs premiere, an alert told fans they could view “Patient Zero” on Spotify Premium, Apple Music or Amazon Music. Notably, Swift has withheld her recent videos from YouTube’s free tier for a couple of days upon release before putting them up there as well, presumably because views on non-paid services do not count toward the consumption totals that fuel the Billboard charts. It will be available on YouTube as of Tuesday, the alert noted.
In advance of the music video’s release, Swift took to her Instagram Stories on Sunday to post a short clip of herself talking to the camera, with a dateline revealing for the first time that the “Patient Zero” video was shot all the way back in March. (Needless to say, no NDA gets respected like a Taylor Swift NDA.) It gives confirmation that she hatched the idea for a VMAs premiere half a year ago, and held onto it as a secret till this date.
Says Swift in the IG clip: “Walking through here and seeing the way that Chivo has lit this and the way the sets are and how brilliantly Ethan has done this set design, I’m kind of rethinking the release of the video. Like, I need to figure a way to get this on TV or something. I’m sort of like: ‘Google, when are the VMAs?'” A caption under the video states the obvious: “Turns out the VMAs are Sept. 27, aka today.”
In that quote, “Chivo” is a nickname for Oscar-winning cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, and “Ethan” refers to Ethan Tobman, her longtime production designer.
Beyond her nominations at the VMAs for “The Life of a Showgirl” and “The Fate of Ophelia,” Swift was given a guaranteed trip to the podium for whatever speech or unveiling she might have in mind when CBS announced that she would be receiving the inaugural Artist Director Honor. The award is given to an artist who is accomplished behind the camera as well as in front of it. Producers have described it as analogous in stature to the VMAs’ traditional Video Vanguard award, while noting that it is an unknown whether any other artists will receive this new honor in the future.
When she came back to accept her award for video of the year for “Ophelia,” she said, “Thank you so much for giving this award to this video… I just I loved making this video because I wanted it to seem like one continuous shot, so I learned a lot about hiding cuts in places. articles.title_orig: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ bows at No. 1, ‘Primetime’ catches $20 million globally
articles.title_zh: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ bows at No. 1, ‘Primetime’ catches $20 million globally
articles.content_orig:
Audiences assembled this weekend for the re-release of Marvel Studios ’ beloved Avengers Endgame: Encore , powering the already record-breaking box office smash to another No. 1 global release , this time as the estimated second highest global debut of all-time for a re-release .
The film brought in an estimated $86 million at the global box office , with $26 million coming from domestic audiences and $60 million from the international box office . That helped power Marvel Studios to $35.075 billion at the box office across its 38 films , furthering its position as the most successful film franchise in history.
The global cumulative box office gross for Avengers: Endgame now stands at $2.885 billion , placing it No. 2 on the all-time box office list , only $39 million behind 20 th Century Studios’ Avatar .
The overwhelming excitement surrounding Avengers Endgame: Encore is a powerful testament to Disney’s unrivaled ability to create epic, enduring stories that fans want to return to again and again.
This special encore presentation also treated fans to an exclusive first look at the highly anticipated Avengers: Doomsday , arriving in theaters December 18 . Doomsday is directed by Endgame helmers Anthony and Joe Russo , and sees the return of many familiar faces from the Marvel Cinematic Universe , including Robert Downey Jr. , not playing his familiar part as Tony Stark/Iron Man, but rather in the new role of Doctor Doom .
Avengers Endgame: Encore features exclusive new footage that directly sets up Doomsday . “We weren’t going to mess with what that movie is,” Endgame and Doomsday co-director Anthony Russo told Marvel.com of the new additions. Instead, the new scenes add depth to the Avengers’ story — while teasing what lies ahead in Doomsday .
And fans of Marvel have plenty more to look forward to, as the studio continues to expand its storytelling universe across not only the next generation of interconnected stories and characters , but also across streaming , products, and experiences at Disney parks, resorts , and cruise ships around the world.
Originally released in 2019, Avengers: Endgame immediately shattered box office records, grossing $1.2 billion in its opening weekend , making it the first and only MPA film in history to surpass $1 billion globally in its opening weekend.
This weekend, Avengers Endgame: Encore opened in over 3,000 theaters , of which over 1,300 were Infinity Vision screens , which accounted for about 52% of the opening weekend figure .
Infinity Vision is a new certification for premium large format (PLF) theaters. The format, done in collaboration with global theatrical exhibition partners, sets a new benchmark for theatrical presentation, certifying auditoriums that meet rigorous technical standards, including a focus on the largest screens for maximum scale, laser projection for superior brightness and clarity, and premium audio formats for fully immersive sound.
The film continues to hold a “Verified Moviegoer” rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with a 96% score across over 1,000 ratings. Additionally, PostTrak polling sits at 5 out of 5 stars from both general and family audiences.
